Location: Zoom

Agenda: Private deployment / VPC networking discovery, region constraints, security requirements, next steps
summary: Customer is evaluating Redwood Private (VPC) for hosting ML inference for ACME's customer-facing product. Main concerns: VPC peering vs PrivateLink, CIDR overlap, egress/ingress controls, cross-region latency, KMS/encryption, and audit logs. AE + SE explained deployment options and tradeoffs. Agreed to share infra details and schedule networking deep dive.
topics: VPC peering vs PrivateLink, private endpoints, route tables, NAT, egress IPs, region availability, data residency, SOC2/KMS, terraform examples, timeline for pilot
transcript:
[00:00] Sara Kim: hey everyone, thanks for making time, I'm Sara from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account. Diego my colleague from solutions is here to run through the network questions and private deployment options.
[00:10] Jill Turner: thanks, Sara. we've got Ravi and Tom and Lina on. main reason for meeting is to understand how Redwood Private would fit into our VPC constraints and security requirements.
[00:22] Diego Martinez: great — high level we support two primary private connectivity patterns: VPC peering (classic) and provider-managed private endpoints (think PrivateLink style). each has tradeoffs.
[00:35] Ravi Patel: can you clarify what you mean by private endpoints? we run in AWS, and we have strict egress rules, plus some accounts are in different regions.
[00:47] Diego Martinez: sure. private endpoints are effectively interface endpoints where traffic stays on AWS backbone via ENIs. they avoid internet NATs, provide stable private IPs. peering is L3 routing between VPCs — simpler for cross-AZ but has CIDR overlap limitations.
[01:05] Tom Nguyen: we cannot change our CIDR block for our prod VPC, there are overlapping ranges across tooling accounts. is that a hard blocker for peering?
[01:15] Diego Martinez: yes if the CIDR overlaps peering won't work; you get route ambiguity. in that case, PrivateLink is recommended. but we can also use a transit VPC or use a proxy in a non-overlapping VPC — more ops overhead.
[01:30] Sara Kim: to add, Redwood Private supports both patterns. choice depends on your networking policy, whether you want full L3 access, and whether you need high-throughput internal traffic.
[01:45] Lina Gomez: what's the perf delta? we worry about latency between our app servers and the inference cluster.
[01:55] Diego Martinez: good question. for same-region PrivateLink the latency overhead is minimal — couple ms. peering is slightly lower latency since it's native routing. cross-region we recommend colocating inference in the same region or using cross-region peering but performance varies; best to benchmark.
[02:15] Ravi Patel: how does egress IPs work? we have firewall allowlists that expect static egress IP ranges.
[02:25] Diego Martinez: with PrivateLink you get stable ENIs in your VPC so egress is your VPC egress as usual. for peering, outbound goes over your VPC as well. if you need fixed egress ranges for logging, we can support NAT gateway patterns or provide a set of known egress IPs in dedicated deployments — we'll need to confirm exact ranges per region.
[02:45] Tom Nguyen: KMS, encryption at rest and in transit? we require customer-managed keys if possible.
[02:55] Sara Kim: yes, we support KMS integration in Private — for our Private deployments we can either bring-your-own-KMS (BYOK) via a customer-managed key in your cloud account or integrate with an HSM on-prem. we'll send the definitive security pack.
[03:12] Jill Turner: audit logs and network flow logs — we need those forwarded to our SIEM. can that be done?
[03:20] Diego Martinez: Redwood Private produces audit logs and we can forward or ship logs to your S3 or CloudWatch logs, and you can pull into the SIEM. for VPC flows, you'd enable VPC flow logs on your side; we can also optionally ingest flow log summaries into our console for debugging.
[03:40] Sara Kim: quick qualification — what's your timeline and success criteria?
[03:45] Lina Gomez: timeline is Q2 pilot ideally; success means comparable latency to our on-prem model, no data exfiltration risk, and SOC2 evidence.
[03:55] Ravi Patel: budget is TBD but we want predictable unit costs; dedicated capacity pricing is important.
[04:03] Diego Martinez: understood. we'll include dedicated pricing + per-token estimates.
[04:10] Jill Turner: we also have a compliance requirement to keep data in eu-west-1 for some customers. can Redwood run Private in specific regions?
[04:20] Sara Kim: yes — Redwood Private can be deployed in customer-chosen regions; we support region constraints and can run in eu-west-1, us-east-1, etc. for on-prem we can also do air-gapped installs.
[04:35] Tom Nguyen: in the case of multiple regions, how do you handle model versioning and rollout?
[04:43] Diego Martinez: we ship a control plane and a local data plane; for Private deployments the model artifacts are pinned per region. we support rollouts and A/B in the console, and you can pin versions per region to avoid cross-region drift.
[05:00] Ravi Patel: what's required from our side network-wise to set up PrivateLink?
[05:08] Diego Martinez: we'll provide a CloudFormation / terraform module that creates the interface endpoint service and the required IAM policy. you need to approve the endpoint and ensure your route tables allow the ENI traffic. we'll send examples.
[05:25] Sara Kim: note: many customers prefer terraform so we'll give you a sample you can drop in.
[05:30] Jill Turner: are there ports or subnets we need to reserve?
[05:35] Diego Martinez: ENIs will need available IPs in the selected subnet; recommend a dedicated /24 or /25 for the service ENIs depending on scale. we'll provide guidance based on expected throughput.
[05:55] Lina Gomez: what about multi-account setups? our infra is split across accounts and we use AWS Organizations.
[06:03] Diego Martinez: PrivateLink works well across accounts — you can create interface endpoints in each account that talk to the same service. Peering across accounts is also fine as long as there is no CIDR overlap. For org-level scale we can use central networking patterns.
[06:18] Ravi Patel: any limitations with Kubernetes clusters talking to the endpoints?
[06:23] Diego Martinez: none specific; in EKS you'd configure endpoints like any other AWS interface endpoint. For on-prem Kubernetes you'll need VPN/Direct Connect into the VPC or run the Private data plane on-prem.
[06:40] Tom Nguyen: if we need IP allowlisting, can we get a small set of stable IPs from Redwood?
[06:48] Diego Martinez: for hosted we cannot promise static IPs across regions; for Dedicated/Private we can negotiate fixed egress IPs via NAT in your VPC. we have examples where customers route through a NAT with allocated Elastic IPs for allowlisting.
[07:05] Sara Kim: let's talk about a hypothetical network diagram — Diego can sketch.
[07:10] Diego Martinez: imagine your app VPC in eu-west-1 with an interface endpoint to our service. traffic flows over the ENI to the data plane which lives in a customer-managed subnet (for Private) or a Redwood-managed subnet in Dedicated. We mirror the connection model but keep control plane API calls optionally over private network.
[07:35] Ravi Patel: control plane — is that managed by Redwood out-of-band or is it inside customer VPC?
[07:42] Diego Martinez: control plane is customer-isolated for Private: it can be in your account or in our control plane with private endpoints back to you. we have both models. many customers want the control plane in a customer-managed VPC for compliance.
[07:55] Jill Turner: do you support bring-your-own-VPN or Direct Connect?
[08:00] Diego Martinez: yes, Direct Connect/ExpressRoute is supported for on-prem connectivity. we also support site-to-site VPN. these are common for regulated customers.
[08:12] Lina Gomez: are there special network policies for GPU clusters? we're concerned about disk egress and model downloads.
[08:20] Diego Martinez: model artifacts can be staged in your S3 or object storage; initial download incurs bandwidth but subsequent serves use local disk/cache. For large models we recommend pre-staging artifacts in-region. We'll share best practices to reduce download times.
[08:40] Ravi Patel: what about KV cache or prefix caching — any network implications?
[08:46] Diego Martinez: the KV cache is local to inference nodes; there's minimal cross-VPC traffic once warmed. only cold starts pull artifacts. If you want shared cache across regions that's more complex and usually avoided.
[09:00] Tom Nguyen: vendor risk — you mentioned we can have private control plane in our account. does that mean logs and keys never leave our account?
[09:08] Diego Martinez: if you choose customer-managed control plane and BYOK, keys and logs stay in your account. Redwood will still operate the product but the data plane and control plane can be configured to meet your isolation needs.
[09:22] Sara Kim: curious — are you leaning to PrivateLink or peering right now?
[09:26] Jill Turner: given CIDR overlap across accounts and multi-region needs, PrivateLink is sounding safer.
[09:33] Ravi Patel: agree. plus we want to avoid touching prod CIDRs.
[09:37] Diego Martinez: makes sense. we'll tailor the terraform to create the interface endpoints in each account and region.
[09:45] Lina Gomez: any constraints on endpoint quotas? AWS has ENI limits per AZ.
[09:50] Diego Martinez: yes. we'll size the number of endpoints and advise reserving IP space. we also support scaling the number of service nodes so ENI counts are predictable.
[10:05] Sara Kim: security checklist — SOC2, pen test, SAML/SSO, RBAC, audit logs. Anything else from your side?
[10:15] Tom Nguyen: we need data residency attestation and a record of subprocessor locations.
[10:22] Sara Kim: we'll include subprocessor list and region mapping in the security pack.
[10:30] Ravi Patel: for terraform examples, do you provide modules per cloud?
[10:35] Diego Martinez: yes we provide terraform modules for AWS, and examples for Azure Private Link equivalents.
[10:40] Jill Turner: ok can you confirm whether we need to route any public traffic through Redwood? we want no public ingress.
[10:48] Diego Martinez: you can configure everything to be internal-only; control plane endpoints can be private, data plane sits in your VPC or connected private network.
[10:55] Lina Gomez: onboarding effort — how long to stand up a pilot?
[11:00] Sara Kim: typical pilot for Private can be 2-4 weeks once we have CIDR and access; longer if you require Direct Connect. We'll propose a timeline in the follow-up.
[11:12] Ravi Patel: any compliance or legal docs to sign before we start?
[11:18] Sara Kim: standard DPA + security addendum; we'll attach them to the next email.
[11:25] Tom Nguyen: about cost, will there be a separate infra fee for Private?
[11:30] Sara Kim: yes Private and Dedicated have a platform fee plus infra/usage. We'll include a breakdown.
[11:36] Diego Martinez: also note quantization and batching options can reduce token cost on the inference side — we'll include tuneups recommendations.
[11:46] Jill Turner: can we run a quick example flow? our app sends request to endpoint, model runs, response returns. what about telemetry?
[11:55] Diego Martinez: traces can be exported via OTLP; we also record per-request latency and per-token cost in the console. If you want traces to flow to your APM, we can configure forwarding.
[12:05] Ravi Patel: do you have a list of IP ranges if we later want to do allowlisting?
[12:10] Sara Kim: for Private we'll provide the recommended NAT/EIP patterns; for hosted it's more fluid. we'll include these notes in the doc.
[12:20] Lina Gomez: are there SLA differences between hosted/dedicated/private?
[12:25] Sara Kim: Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency targets. Private's SLA can be negotiated in the enterprise contract, especially if we're running in your account.
[12:35] Tom Nguyen: we also need to know what happens in failover scenarios — do you support regional fallback?
[12:41] Diego Martinez: yes — you can configure cross-region fallback to another compatible model or region; routing policies can failover to hosted if private capacity is constrained. We'll show the policy examples.
[12:55] Jill Turner: any gotchas with service quotas or account limits?
[12:59] Diego Martinez: mostly ENI quotas, EIP limits, and NAT throughput. We recommend coordinating with your cloud infra team to reserve quotas before pilot.
[13:15] Sara Kim: ok let's recap action items and timeline.
[13:20] Sara Kim: Diego will prepare terraform + endpoint examples; i'll send pricing and security pack; Jill will provide CIDR and account info. target next call: networking deep dive week of 2/3.
[13:35] Jill Turner: sounds good. can you include a checklist for prerequisites?
[13:40] Diego Martinez: yes: CIDR ranges, target subnets for ENIs, IAM role for terraform, logs/siem endpoints, any Direct Connect info.
[13:50] Ravi Patel: we have a separate networking team, we'll invite them to the next meeting.
[13:55] Lina Gomez: thanks, that helps.
[14:00] Sara Kim: any final questions?
[14:05] Tom Nguyen: please include a simple diagram in the follow-up email.
[14:10] Sara Kim: will do. thanks everyone.
[14:15] Jill Turner: thanks all.
[14:18] END OF TRANSCRIPT (note: transcription imperfect; some words may be misrecognized)
